summary: Normalised the second asymmetry. `SummonSession._attribute` now copies the kernel's `point` into `summonSeed` (and `otherPoint` into `otherSummonSeed` on a `batch` refusal) when the refusal does not already carry one, so a renderer doing highlight(rf.summonSeed) works on both verbs instead of silently highlighting nothing on the summons the player actually attempted. ADD, never rename: `point`/`otherPoint` keep their values, so no caller had to be found. `closure`/`nav` are deliberately exempt — they carry `points` (plural) and no index, and inventing one would be a lie. The module header gained a `summonSeed` section paralleling the `first`/`refusal` one. In the gate, §10's field block was rewritten rather than deleted: the two 'place names point and NOT summonSeed' assertions became 'names both, and they agree'; the preview side still pins that it gains no batch index. Added: range checks on both verbs, the place-path `summonSeed === point` copy check, a `batch` block asserting `otherSummonSeed === otherPoint` and that 'self' and 'batch' name the SAME PAIRS of the shape, a `hull` block on section 7's out-of-hull cube, the closure/nav exemption asserted directly against `_attribute`, and three controls on the normalisation itself (copied not recomputed, an existing summonSeed never overwritten, an index-less refusal gains none). THE ASSERTION THAT JUSTIFIES THE TICKET is the cross-verb one: one geometry through both verbs, both naming index 2 — the claim no per-verb field check can make. HONESTLY: I had no Bash, so NEITHER FILE WAS RUN. Every index was derived by hand against the exact sources (foamworld.js:925-948, placement.mjs:236-258) and against numbers sections 4 and 8 of this same gate already prove; two fixtures (the tiny cube's pair set, the hull fixture's index set) were checked for floating-point boundary risk and both clear the 1.5m threshold by >0.015. Section 8 was touched by exactly one line — `const TINY_AT` became an assignment to a hoisted `let`, mirroring the existing `LANDED` pattern — so §10 can borrow its fixture instead of siting a second one.

learned.title: Cross-verb index agreement must be compared as a SET, not a list — legalSeed reports the nearest colliding seed, the kernel reports every colliding pair
learned.body:
The obvious way to assert 'both verbs name the same part of the shape' is to compare the two lists of `summonSeed`. That is only sound on a fixture with exactly one collision, and it is a trap on any other.

THE MECHANISM. `legalSeed` calls `nearestSeed` and returns AT MOST ONE refusal per summon seed — the closest pocket seed, and only if it is inside the gap. `reformPocketAll` loops `for k over pocket.seeds` and pushes a refusal for EVERY colliding pair. So a summon seed sitting between two close pocket seeds produces:

    preview  [ 5 ]
    place    [ 5, 5 ]

Same blame, different multiplicity, and a list comparison calls that a disagreement. It is not one: the two verbs are answering slightly different questions (which seed is worst vs which pairs are illegal) and both answers are correct.

This mattered concretely here. The FIX.c2 fixture is safe for a LIST comparison and I asserted it as one, because section 4 of this same gate already derives by hand that exactly one pair of the fourteen seeds is under 1.5m. The moment I added a hull fixture — a cube centred at x=0.5, whose centre and −x neighbour are both outside the wall while its other five seeds are wherever the foam left them — the list form would have been a flake generator: any one of those five landing near two pocket seeds produces a duplicate on the place side only. So that block compares `[...new Set(...)].sort()` and says why in a comment.

THE TRANSFERABLE SHAPE. When two implementations of the same predicate are asserted to agree, first ask what each one's output is a list OF. 'Which things are wrong' and 'which pairs are wrong' project onto the same set of blamed indices and onto different multisets. Comparing the richer structure looks stricter and is simply wrong — it fails correct work, which this ledger already records as worse than no checker.

Where the multiplicity IS the interesting claim, compare it deliberately: the tiny-cube block compares `summonSeed`-`otherSummonSeed` PAIRS between 'self' and 'batch', because there both sides enumerate over i<j and the pair sets really must be identical.

learned.title: The tiny-cube self/batch pair set is the strongest cross-verb check available, and it is safe from the float boundary by 0.017
learned.body:
The `batch` half of this ticket needs a fixture where a summon fights itself. Section 8's tiny cube (r=0.5 at a centre 3.5m clear of every seed) is the one that already exists, and it turns out to support a much stronger assertion than 'both refuse'.

`placement.mjs`'s self loop and the kernel's batch loop both enumerate i<j over the same seven seeds with the same aniso, so after normalisation the two must name the IDENTICAL SET OF PAIRS — not merely the same count, and not merely the same reason. The gate compares `summonSeed-otherSummonSeed` strings, sorted.

Working the arithmetic out was worth it because it also settles the boundary question. Cube at r=0.5, aniso 2.2, so a y offset scales by sqrt(2.2)=1.4832. Seeds are the centre plus ±x, ±y, ±z at unscaled distance 1.0. Every pair gap:

    centre↔±x, ±z      1.0000   < 1.5   refused  (4 pairs)
    centre↔±y          1.4832   < 1.5   refused  (2 pairs)
    x↔z cross          1.4142   < 1.5   refused  (4 pairs)
    x↔y, z↔y           1.7889   > 1.5   legal
    +x↔−x, +z↔−z       2.0000   > 1.5   legal
    +y↔−y              2.9665   > 1.5   legal

Ten refused pairs, and the closest approach to the threshold is 1.4832 — 0.017 below. That matters because the two layers compare DIFFERENTLY: `placement.mjs` tests `gap < minSeedGap` on the square root, the kernel tests `sq < MIN_SEED_GAP_SQ` on the square. Those two are equivalent in exact arithmetic and can disagree in floating point for a pair sitting within an ulp or two of 1.5. Nothing here is within 0.015, so the pair sets cannot diverge for rounding reasons and the equality assertion is safe rather than lucky.

General shape: an assertion that two differently-formed comparisons agree is only as sound as the closest fixture point to the threshold. Compute that distance before asserting equality of two predicate outputs — it is one line of arithmetic and it is the difference between a gate and a coin toss.

learned.title: The closure/nav exemption is asserted against `_attribute` directly, not left to a fixture that may never fire
learned.body:
The ticket requires the gate to assert that `closure` and `nav` refusals still carry no index. Neither is decidable before the rebuild — `summon-session.mjs`'s own header says so — so on this fixture they may simply never occur, and a loop over real refusals that finds none asserts nothing while printing ticks.

I chose to call `S._attribute({ reason: 'closure', points: [...] })` directly and assert `summonSeed === undefined` and `blame === 'foam'`. That is a deterministic check of the exclusion on every run.

WHAT I REJECTED: (a) the structural-scan-only form, which is vacuous whenever the fixture is clean — this is the 'a check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from a check that passes' shape the ledger already records; (b) `summon-view.selftest.mjs`'s precedent of saying out loud that a blame class may be unreachable and checking it structurally — right for a RENDERER, whose input is whatever the session hands it, but wrong here, because the exemption is a property of one branch of one function and that function is directly callable.

THE COST, stated plainly: the gate now reaches into a method whose name starts with an underscore, so a future refactor that renames or inlines `_attribute` breaks the gate for a reason that is not a regression. I judged that acceptable because this file already reaches into `S.pocket`, `G.ownerOf` and `G.originCount`, and because the alternative is an assertion that is silently vacuous — which is strictly worse than one that is loudly coupled. Both forms are present: the direct call, plus a scan of real refusals that logs how many actually arose, so the coupling is belt-and-braces rather than the only check.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: `reformPocketAll` gaining a way to force a closure failure deterministically from a fixture. Then the real-refusal scan becomes non-vacuous and the direct call can go.

learned.title: Neither file was run (no Bash) — recording only what is specific to THIS turn's risk, which is a fixture claim rather than arithmetic
learned.body:
The standing 'gate unverifiable in-turn' recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it. I am not restating it.

What is specific here: the implementation change is three lines and essentially unfailable (two guarded copies into a spread object). ALL the residual risk is in the gate's new FIXTURE CLAIMS, and there are exactly four:

  1. `nSeeds === 7` — a cube is centre plus six faces; section 6 of this same file already asserts `plantedCount === 7`.
  2. Both verbs name `[2]` for FIX.c2 — section 4 derives the 1.4m pair by hand and already asserts `f.point === 2` on the identical geometry; my claim is that the preview side names the same 2, which follows from `place()` handing `con.seeds` in order.
  3. `hullOf === [0, 2]` for the cube at [0.5, 18.9, 38] — hand-derived: `hullBounds` is x∈[1,W−1] and the cube's axis neighbours sit at exactly ±3.2 (q=1 for a unit axis normal, so aniso cannot move them), giving centre x=0.5 and −x x=−2.7 outside, +x x=3.7 inside, and y=18.9±3.2 / z=38±3.2 comfortably inside. Section 7 already asserts that this point's FIRST refusal is a hull with wall B4, which pins the centre; index 2 follows from the same table.
  4. The self/batch pair sets are equal — filed as its own finding with the arithmetic.

Each of the four is a claim about the FIXTURE, so a wrong one fails with a message naming the fixture rather than the module. That was deliberate: every new assertion prints the values it compared, so a red gate says 'preview [0,2], place [0,2,5]' rather than 'false'.

Two mechanical passes that need no shell were run over the added text, because arithmetic is not the only way an unrun test file dies: no backtick nested inside a template literal (the only interpolations are `'${rf.reason}'`-style with SINGLE quotes) and no ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string (the three added single-quoted messages use the typographic apostrophe, matching house style). Either would make the file fail to PARSE, at which point not one assertion runs and the failure reads like an unrelated typo.

propose.title: Highlight the offending part of the shape in the summon panel — the payoff of the summonSeed normalisation, and it changes what a visitor sees
Pin which fields each refusal reason carries, per reason — legalSummon's docstring promises `summonSeed` on EVERY refusal and the `metric` refusal does not have one
propose.body:
THE DEFECT, already recorded as a finding and still open. `placement.mjs`'s `legalSummon` header states: 'Every refusal carries `summonSeed` — the index within `con.seeds`, where 0 is the centre — so a caller can light up the offending part of the shape.' The `metric` refusal, pushed twelve lines below that sentence, carries only `{ ok, reason, conAniso, pocketAniso }`.

Omitting it is CORRECT — a metric mismatch is a property of the whole constellation and there is no single seed to blame — so this is not a bug in the predicate. It is a bug in the sentence, and the cost lands on exactly the caller the sentence was written for: a UI that trusts it writes `refusals.map(r => highlight(r.summonSeed))`, lights up `undefined` and shows nothing, silently, on the one refusal it is least likely to have a fixture for. lp-fcf387 has just made that renderer worth writing, which is what promotes this from a note to a ticket.

THE WORK, two halves and the second is the one that lasts:
  1. One word in the docstring: 'every PER-SEED refusal'. Also state which fields the `metric` refusal DOES carry.
  2. A table-driven assertion in `plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs`: for each reason `legalSummon` can emit — metric, hull, seed, self — assert the EXACT sorted key set of the refusal object. A field list that no test reads is a field list that drifts, and this is the second consumer (after `level.mjs`) to build a walk over refusals from that paragraph.

WHY A LOOSER CHECK WOULD NOT DO: asserting 'a hull refusal has a wall' catches nothing, because it is satisfied by every implementation that has ever existed. The claim that bites is the exact key SET, because it fails when a field is ADDED as well as when one is removed — and a silently added field is how the `summonSeed`/`point` divergence survived as long as it did.

NOTE ON REACHING `metric`: `summonAt` takes aniso from the pocket, which makes the metric refusal unreachable through it by construction. The fixture must build a constellation by hand with a deliberately wrong aniso and pass it to `legalSummon` directly — `placement.selftest.mjs` already has a block that does exactly this, so the fixture exists.

WHY class-a: `plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs` exists and passes today. BOUNDED PATHS: plant/placement.mjs, plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs.
